philosophical-zombies: A philosophical zombie is an imagined being physically and behaviorally identical to a normal human but wholly lacking conscious experience—there is nothing it is like to be it, even as it walks, talks, and reacts exactly as we do. David Chalmers uses the apparent conceivability of such creatures to argue that consciousness cannot be fully explained by physical facts alone, since a complete account of brain and behavior would leave the presence of subjective experience unexplained. The thought experiment sharpens the so-called hard problem of consciousness and remains a central weapon in debates between physicalists and their critics.
extended-mind: The extended mind thesis, proposed by Andy Clark and David Chalmers, holds that the mind is not confined to the brain or even the body but can literally extend into the environment when external tools become integrated into our cognitive processes. Their famous example imagines a man who relies on a notebook to store beliefs the way others rely on biological memory; if the notebook functions in the same role, they argue, it counts as part of his mind. The view challenges the intuitive boundary of skull and skin and has shaped discussions of cognition, technology, and personal identity.
intentional-stance: The intentional stance is Daniel Dennett's term for the strategy of predicting a system's behavior by treating it as a rational agent that has beliefs, desires, and goals. Rather than asking whether a thermostat, animal, or person really has mental states in some deep metaphysical sense, we adopt the stance because doing so yields reliable predictions of what the system will do. For Dennett, the usefulness and success of this interpretive strategy is what it means to have beliefs and desires, offering a deflationary but robust account of mind.
cartesian-theater: The Cartesian theater is Daniel Dennett's derisive label for a mistaken picture of consciousness in which there is a central place in the brain where everything 'comes together' and is presented to an inner observer, as if on a screen. Dennett argues this image is an incoherent remnant of Cartesian dualism, since it merely relocates the puzzle of experience to a homunculus who would need its own inner theater in turn. In its place he proposes a 'multiple drafts' model, on which mental content is distributed across parallel processes with no single finish line where consciousness happens.
language-games: A language game, in Ludwig Wittgenstein's later philosophy, is a rule-governed activity in which words gain their meaning from the way they are used within a shared form of life, such as giving orders, telling jokes, or reporting an event. Wittgenstein introduced the idea to counter the view that words function chiefly by naming objects, arguing instead that meaning is inseparable from practice and context. The notion underlies his claim that many philosophical confusions arise from taking language out of the settings in which it actually works.
private-language: The private language argument, developed in Wittgenstein's Philosophical Investigations, contends that a language whose words refer to purely private, inwardly known sensations—intelligible in principle to no one but the speaker—is impossible. Because such a language would offer no public criteria for using a term correctly, there could be no genuine distinction between following a rule and merely seeming to, and so no real meaning at all. The argument targets the assumption that mental terms get their sense by private ostension and reshapes debates about the relation between language, mind, and the shared world.
russells-teapot: Russell's teapot is an analogy devised by Bertrand Russell to argue that the burden of proof lies with the person making an unfalsifiable claim, not with those who doubt it. Russell imagined asserting that a china teapot orbits the Sun somewhere between Earth and Mars, too small to be detected by any telescope; the claim cannot be disproved, yet no one is thereby obliged to believe it. He used the image to challenge the idea that skeptics must refute religious or other extraordinary assertions rather than the claimants having to support them.
naturalistic-fallacy: The naturalistic fallacy is G. E. Moore's charge that it is a mistake to define moral goodness in terms of any natural property, such as pleasure, desire, or evolutionary fitness. In Principia Ethica he argued that 'good' names a simple, non-natural quality that cannot be reduced to factual descriptions, and offered the 'open question argument': for any proposed natural definition, it remains sensibly open to ask whether things with that property are really good. The claim influenced twentieth-century metaethics and is often linked to the broader worry about deriving values from facts.
sense-reference: Sense and reference is the distinction Gottlob Frege drew to explain how expressions relate to the world and to our understanding of them. The reference of a term is the object it stands for, while its sense is the particular mode of presentation, the way that object is given to us. Frege illustrated this with 'the morning star' and 'the evening star,' which share a reference (Venus) but differ in sense, thereby explaining why identity statements can be informative rather than trivial, and laying a foundation for modern philosophy of language.
quine-indeterminacy: The indeterminacy of translation is W. V. O. Quine's thesis that there is no uniquely correct way to translate one language into another, because incompatible translation manuals can each fit all possible behavioral evidence equally well. In his 'radical translation' scenario, a linguist confronting an unknown tongue could never fix, from observation alone, whether a native term means 'rabbit' or 'undetached rabbit part.' Quine drew from this the more radical conclusion that facts about meaning are not fully determined by any facts at all, unsettling assumptions about linguistic and mental content.
web-of-belief: The web of belief is Quine's metaphor for the way our beliefs form an interconnected system that faces experience as a whole rather than one claim at a time. Observations impinge on the periphery of the web, while logical and mathematical principles sit near the resistant center; when evidence conflicts with the system, we may revise it at many different points, and no belief is in principle immune to revision. The picture rejects a sharp line between analytic and synthetic truths and reframes knowledge as a holistic, revisable structure.
kripke-naming: In Naming and Necessity, Saul Kripke argued that proper names are 'rigid designators,' picking out the same individual in every possible situation in which that individual exists, rather than functioning as disguised descriptions. On this view a name like 'Aristotle' refers to the same person even in counterfactual scenarios where he did none of the things we associate with him, its reference secured by a causal-historical chain reaching back to an initial baptism. Kripke's account overturned the dominant descriptivist theory and introduced influential notions of necessary yet a posteriori truth.
possible-worlds: Possible worlds are complete alternative ways things might have been, used in logic and metaphysics to analyze claims about necessity and possibility: a statement is necessary if it holds in all possible worlds and possible if it holds in at least one. David Lewis defended the striking doctrine of modal realism, on which these worlds are not mere abstractions or fictions but concrete realities as fully existent as our own, spatiotemporally isolated from us. Though few accept Lewis's full realism, possible-worlds talk has become an indispensable tool across philosophy of language, modality, and counterfactual reasoning.
category-mistake: A category mistake, a notion introduced by Gilbert Ryle, occurs when something is placed in a logical category to which it does not belong, as when a visitor shown the colleges and library asks to be shown 'the University' as if it were a further building. Ryle used the idea to diagnose confusions in philosophy, arguing that many puzzles arise from treating concepts of one type as though they were of another. The device is central to his critique of the mind as a separate inner substance.
ghost-in-the-machine: 'The ghost in the machine' is Gilbert Ryle's mocking phrase for the Cartesian doctrine that a person consists of a physical body inhabited by a distinct, immaterial mind. In The Concept of Mind he argued that this dualism rests on a category mistake, wrongly treating mental life as a hidden inner theater causally driving bodily movements. In its place Ryle urged that talk of mind refers to patterns of behavior and dispositions rather than to a private ghostly substance, a view that helped shape philosophical behaviorism.
